---- eval/simulator/README.md
     1	# Simulator results
     2	
     3	How often does the lineup name the right commit, for a given number of replays? This folder answers that with simulated cases, where the culprit is known.
     4	
     5	Each case has 40 suspect commits and one culprit picked at random. Every point is 500 cases. Three methods get the same cases and the same replay budget:
     6	
     7	- The statistical bisect in `whodunit/lineup.py`. It names a commit only when it is 95% sure, and otherwise hands back the suspects that remain with their probabilities.
     8	- Plain bisect with repeats. It replays each commit as many times as the budget allows and calls the commit bad on the first failure.
     9	- Plain bisect with one replay per commit, which is what `git bisect run` does.
    10	
    11	To regenerate everything here, run `uv run python -m whodunit.simulate --out eval/simulator`. It takes about two minutes. `tables.md` has every number behind the charts, and `results.json` has the raw counts.
    12	
    13	## When good commits never fail
    14	
    15	![Accuracy against replay budget when good commits never fail](accuracy-clean-baseline.svg)
    16	
    17	Plain bisect with repeats wins here at every budget. For a bug that fails 30% of the time, 80 replays get it to 97% while the statistical bisect names the right commit in 67% of cases. The statistical bisect needs 160 replays to reach 93%.
    18	
    19	The reason is that plain bisect with repeats assumes a single failure convicts a commit, and in this world that is true. The statistical bisect does not assume it. It starts out believing a good commit fails about 5% of the time and spends replays finding out.
    20	
    21	Two things are worth knowing before picking plain bisect on that basis. Its mistakes are silent: with 40 replays on the 30% bug it names the wrong commit in 26% of cases and gives no sign of it, where the statistical bisect names the wrong one in 2% and says "not sure yet" in the rest. And the dashed line shows the statistical bisect's top suspect is right in 91% of cases at 80 replays, so most of its "not sure yet" answers are pointing at the culprit already.
    22	
    23	Plain bisect with one replay per commit is right 10% of the time on the 30% bug, at any budget.
    24	
    25	## When good commits fail 5% of the time on their own
    26	
    27	![Accuracy against replay budget when good commits fail 5% of the time](accuracy-flaky-baseline.svg)
    28	
    29	Agents are rarely this clean. Give every good commit a 5% chance of failing by itself and plain bisect with repeats falls apart, and more replays make it worse. On the 30% bug it is right in 31% of cases with 40 replays and 4% with 320, because every extra replay of an innocent commit is another chance for a stray failure to convict it. Even a bug that fails every time is found in only 46% of cases at 40 replays.
    30	
    31	The statistical bisect holds up. On the 30% bug it names the right commit in 60% of cases with 160 replays and 84% with 320. On a bug that fails every time it is right in 99% of cases and uses about 21 replays.
    32	
    33	## Where it falls short
    34	
    35	- A bug that fails 20% of the time on a flaky baseline is named in only 46% of cases, even with 320 replays. The top suspect is right in 70%.
    36	- The 95% bar is not always met. Across the cells, the share of cases with a wrong accusation runs from 0% to 7%, and the 7% is the 30% bug on a flaky baseline at 320 replays. The model assumes one change point and two fixed failure rates, and the prior on the good rate is a guess.
    37	- These are simulated commits with independent replays. Real replays share a model provider and a machine, so their failures can come in bursts, which this does not capture.
    38	- Small budgets are spent mostly on warming up. Below about 30 replays the statistical bisect rarely names anyone unless the bug fails every time.
    39	
    40	## What changed from the first design
    41	
    42	Two things, both found by simulating the 30% bug across 40 suspects with 300 replays allowed.
    43	
    44	The first version put a uniform prior on both failure rates, so it had to learn from scratch that good commits mostly pass. It solved 59% of cases. Starting from the belief that a good commit fails about 5% of the time, loosely held, took that to 93%.
    45	
    46	The brief said to test the commit that splits the posterior mass most evenly. The code now defaults to the replay with the highest expected information gain, and keeps the even split as `how="split"`. With the uniform prior the difference was large, 92% against 59%. With the current prior it is small: 282 cases solved against 280 out of 300, using 79 replays on average against 83. So the prior did the work, and the choice of picker barely matters.
---- eval/sealed/README.md
     1	# Sealed eval, 11 October 2026
     2	
     3	Five regressions were planted in the refund agent's history by a second coding session, through ordinary requests to fresh coding sessions. It wrote the answer key, and the key's SHA-256 was committed in 4c45f7f before Whodunit ran on any case. `eval/score.py` checks the key against that hash before scoring. The key was added to git only after every case had been run.
     4	
     5	Replays ran on the hackathon gateway's small model, three at a time.
     6	
     7	## Result
     8	
     9	With 120 replays allowed per case: 3 of 5 solved, 0 wrong accusations, 2 cases where nobody was named.
    10	
    11	The two open cases were then resumed from their own replays with up to 200 more allowed: 5 of 5 solved, 0 wrong accusations.
    12	
    13	| Case | Rate the second session measured | Rate Whodunit estimated | At 120 replays | In the end | Replays | Commits replayed | Suspects |
    14	| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
    15	| cents-off | 100% | 93% | solved | solved | 21 | 5 | 13 |
    16	| wrong-order-refunded | 30% | 12% | nobody named | solved | 168 | 9 | 12 |
    17	| half-done-batch | 25% | 14% | nobody named | solved | 168 | 10 | 15 |
    18	| strangers-paid | 72% | 59% | solved | solved | 30 | 5 | 11 |
    19	| turned-away | 100% | 93% | solved | solved | 24 | 6 | 14 |
    20	
    21	The rate Whodunit estimates is a posterior mean, so after only a few replays it sits below 100% even for a bug that fails every time.
    22	
    23	## What it cost
    24	
    25	Replay spend on the gateway, estimated from token counts at list prices, came to about $1.91 for all five cases:
    26	
    27	- cents-off: about $0.08 (61,267 tokens)
    28	- wrong-order-refunded: about $0.57 (438,034 tokens)
    29	- half-done-batch: about $1.04 (795,110 tokens)
    30	- strangers-paid: about $0.10 (78,530 tokens)
    31	- turned-away: about $0.12 (100,111 tokens)
    32	
    33	## What this does and does not show
    34	
    35	- No commit was wrongly accused, at either budget. On `half-done-batch` the top suspect at 120 replays was the wrong commit, at 53%, and Whodunit named nobody. That is the behaviour the 95% bar is for.
    36	- The two cases it could not close at 120 replays are the two that fail least often. Whodunit put them at 12% and 14%, where the second session had measured 30% and 25% from a handful of probes. A bug that rare needs a lot of replays whatever the method.
    37	- The ranges are short, 11 to 15 suspects. On ranges this size a careful scan from the oldest commit would have replayed about as many commits as Whodunit did, so this eval says little about savings on long histories. The simulator in `eval/simulator` covers 40 suspects.
    38	- Five cases is a small sample. It is enough to say the pipeline works on a history it did not write, and not enough to put a number on accuracy.
    39	- Each case has one planted regression inside its range, by design. Two regressions that touch the same inputs in one range are outside what the model assumes.
    40	
    41	## What happened after the culprits were named
    42	
    43	The owner's ruling was patch for all three kinds of change involved. A fix counts as proven when its failure rate is back within 5 points of the rate before the culprit, at 95%.
    44	
    45	| Case | Outcome | Tries | Replays of the final fix |
    46	| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
    47	| cents-off | patched and proven | 1 | 0 failures in 30 |
    48	| strangers-paid | patched and proven | 1 | 0 failures in 30 |
    49	| wrong-order-refunded | patched and proven | 1 | 0 failures in 36 |
    50	| turned-away | two patches not proven, then reverted and proven | 3 | 0 failures in 30 |
    51	| half-done-batch | not fixed | 3 | two patches left 5 failures in 90 each, and the revert conflicts |
    52	
    53	So four of five were closed, one of them only by giving up on the patch the owner asked for, and one was left open and says so.
    54	
    55	## The same culprit across the whole history
    56	
    57	`cases/whole-history.toml` takes the `strangers-paid` regression and widens the range to the whole grown history, 57 suspects. With alibis from entire-graph for 22 of them and 18 ordinary runs as evidence, 20 replays across 5 commits named the culprit at 99.8%. A scan from the oldest suspect would have tested 37 commits. This is the run that speaks to savings on a longer history, and it is one run.
    58	
    59	## Against plain bisect with retries
    60	
    61	The same five cases were then given to plain bisect, with each commit replayed up to 5 times over and called bad on the first failure. It ran once per case, so this is one sample and not a rate.
    62	
    63	| Case | Plain bisect, 5 retries | Its replays | Statistical bisect | Its replays |
    64	| --- | --- | ---: | --- | ---: |
    65	| cents-off | right | 15 | right | 21 |
    66	| strangers-paid | right | 15 | right | 30 |
    67	| turned-away | right | 25 | right | 24 |
    68	| wrong-order-refunded | wrong commit named | 19 | right | 168 |
    69	| half-done-batch | could not start: the bad ref passed 10 replays in a row | 10 | right | 168 |
    70	
    71	On the three bugs that fail most of the time, plain bisect was right and used 55 replays in all against 75. That matches the simulator: with a clean baseline, and this one was clean (0 failures in 211 replays of commits before a culprit), plain bisect with retries is the cheaper tool.
    72	
    73	On the two bugs that fail about one run in eight, it went wrong in the two ways it can. For `wrong-order-refunded` a bad commit passed all 5 tries, the search went the wrong way, and it named an innocent commit three places from the real one, with nothing to say it was unsure. For `half-done-batch` the bad ref itself passed 10 replays in a row, so there was nothing to bisect.
    74	
    75	More retries would have fixed both, at a cost. The trouble is that the number has to be picked before the failure rate is known. The statistical bisect does not need it picked: it spent 21 to 30 replays on the frequent bugs and 168 on the rare ones, and on the rare ones it said "not sure yet" at 120 instead of naming someone.

That commit's trailer looks fine. Now I'm thinking through the rule check for brief.py — rejecting briefs claiming "always" or "deterministic" when the measured rate is under 95%, which means I need to extend Evidence to carry the actual numeric rate rather than just descriptive words.

The tricky part is which rate counts as "measured." Whodunit's failure rate is a posterior mean from a Beta(1,1) prior, so a bug that truly fails every time can still sit at 93% after only 13 replays — meaning a brief that correctly says "always" would get rejected under a naive 95% threshold. That matches the sealed README's warning that the posterior mean sits below 100% even for deterministic bugs after few replays, so I need to account for this when deciding whether "always" claims are actually unsupported by the evidence.

The cleanest principle is that the brief must never contradict the number printed next to it, so I'll use the lineup's reported rate plus raw counts in the re-ask prompt, like "N failures in M replays." For the cents-off case, instead of "every time," the model should say something like "failed in all 13 replays," which is true and avoids the flagged words (always, every time, deterministic). If the model still insists after a second rejection, I need to decide whether to drop the offending sentences or fall back to a template.

I'll allow one retry, and if the absolute claim persists, cut the offending sentences and log them under `dropped` with a reason, just like citation trimming. If nothing survives after trimming, fall back to the template -- preserving the invariant that no published sentence makes an absolute claim unsupported by the data. I also need to guard against false positives from negations like "not always" or "never deterministic," so the regex catching absolute terms should skip matches preceded closely by negation words like "not," "never," or "instead of."

I also need to guard against "non-deterministic" matching the "deterministic" pattern via word boundary after the hyphen, so I'm adding a negative lookbehind for "non"/"non-" prefixes, plus a negation check for words like "not", "never", "without" appearing just before the absolute term, and I should apply the same check to headlines too. Writing the regex pattern...

I need to also match phrases like "every single time/run/replay," "each time," "deterministically," "invariably," "without fail," and "100%," while being cautious about edge cases like "100%" being legitimately cited or "every replay" being technically true depending on the actual pass rate — I'll keep the pattern focused on time/run-based phrasing rather than trying to cover every variant.

Now I'm sketching the detection function that flags sentences making absolute claims when the measured rate falls below 95%, and wiring it into the brief-writing flow: generate an answer, parse and check citations, then if the evidence's rate is below the always-needs-hedging threshold, scan for absolute claims. If found, I re-prompt the model with a rejection message pointing out the mismatch between its claim and the actual measurements, then re-check the new answer — dropping any sentences that still make unsupported absolute claims and recording them, while handling the case where the headline itself is the offending claim.

I want the brief to record a "rejected" list capturing offending sentences from earlier rejected drafts, so the page can transparently note that a draft was rejected for overstating certainty. I'm also thinking through extending the Evidence structure with numeric fields like rate_from and rate_before, and reconsidering how to compute replay/failure counts — noting that the simple _sides helper only counts replays, not full witnessed traffic, which matters since the lineup's failure rate includes more than that.

Since traffic_runs and traffic_failures are only tracked in total rather than split by side, I'll word the measured evidence to state both: replay counts split by side, plus a combined estimate with ordinary traffic folded in. I'll add a system prompt rule forbidding absolute language like "always" or "deterministically" unless the measured rate from the culprit onward is 95% or higher, requiring the actual rate to be cited instead — enforced by the rule checker. The template brief doesn't make rate claims, so that's fine as is.

I also need to think through the citation rule that every id-shaped token in a sentence must resolve: I'm working out a regex for hex strings of the right length while avoiding false positives like hex-spelled words ("deadbeef", "defaced") versus legitimate all-digit or mixed hex ids, considering whether to require at least one digit and one letter to distinguish real ids from plain numbers or hex words.

Pure-letter tokens like "deadbeef" would slip through since they're all letters, but that's rare enough not to worry about, while all-digit 8+ character tokens should be flagged unless they resolve to something citable.

To limit false positives, I'll narrow "id-shaped" digit tokens to exact lengths like 8 or 12 characters, since a stray 8-digit number is unlikely in normal prose. The citation check itself should extend to cut any sentence containing an in-text id-shaped token that doesn't resolve against the evidence's citable set.

I'm also considering a one-time re-ask loop: if a sentence gets cut for an unresolvable id, surface the mistyped ids to the model and let it correct them before final cutting. And for ids that do resolve in-text but aren't explicitly cited, I'm weighing whether to union them into the sentence's citation set so later footnoting covers everything named.

I'm also refining the prefix-matching rule for `real()` — matching cite tokens against known ids using bidirectional prefix checks with a minimum length threshold, applied the same way to in-text ids. Separately, factual errors like misdescribed library behavior aren't catchable by any citation rule, so I'm thinking the fix needs to come from a system-level instruction telling the model not to assert general language/library behavior unless it's actually grounded in the evidence.

Now I'm double-checking Python's actual rounding behavior before rewriting the brief: round() uses banker's rounding on exact halves (round(0.5)=0, round(1.5)=2, round(2.5)=2), but for non-exact values like 64.75 or 129.99 it rounds normally since they aren't halfway cases. So the claim "rounds 0.5 and above up" is inaccurate, and I need to make sure the rewritten brief doesn't repeat that error.

For actually regenerating the brief, running `whodunit brief` again would trigger neatroots to re-gather evidence, and since the failing_run is unset this could kick off real-model replays through the gateway, costing a bit each time. I'm thinking it'd be better to add a `--from-record` flag so the brief can be rewritten purely from the evidence already captured, without re-invoking neatroots or triggering new replays.

Now I'm sketching a function to check claims in a brief against the measured evidence, returning a list of problem descriptions, and the drafting flow that prompts the LLM and extracts the JSON answer from its response.

I want objections to classify issues like missing citations, references to things not present in the evidence, or exaggerated language against the real measured failure rate. I'll keep `check_citations` as the public test-facing function but extend it to cover in-text ids too, while adding a separate `check_rates` for the absolute-claims rule, with `write_brief` combining both. Now I'm sketching how `write_brief` retries the draft when unbacked claims are found -- generating a brief, checking it for absolute claims, regenerating with objections if any exist, then filtering out sentences that still make the bad claim, moving them into the dropped list.

I'm sketching out tests confirming the rewrite loop replaces absolute claims with correct percentages and flags rejected sentences, covering edge cases like 97% rounding to "always" and negations like "does not always" being acceptable. For the CLI, I'm planning to restructure the measured-value logic into a helper function and add a `--from-record` flag, threading `from_record` through the `investigate` command too.

I'm drafting the measured-text template that reports replay counts, failure ratios before and after the culprit, optional traffic-run stats, and the final estimated failure rates as percentages.

I'm extending check_citations so every id-shaped token in sentence text—span ids, commit hashes, checkpoint ids—must resolve to something real, which means writing a helper to extract those tokens and cross-check them.

Unresolved ids cause the sentence to be dropped with a "not in evidence" problem, while resolved in-text ids get folded into the citation list. I'm also deciding how headline-level unresolvable ids should be handled, probably triggering an objection and falling back to a template headline on repeated failure, and shaping the return value with headline, sentences, dropped, and objections fields so the page renderer and re-ask logic can use them.

Now I'm working out whether unresolvable in-text ids should also feed into the re-ask step alongside rate objections, while missing-citation sentences still just get cut silently like before. I'm restructuring write_brief so it pops the unresolved problems off the draft, combines them with other rejection reasons, and decides whether to trigger a re-ask or just drop those sentences.

I'm wrestling with double-counting: if a sentence shows up in both the first draft's dropped list and the rejected list sent for re-ask, it could get counted twice in the final record. I'm simplifying by making the final dropped count reflect only what the second draft actually cut, rather than merging drops across both drafts.

Still better, but sentence 2 is misleading since the request explicitly asked to round to the nearest whole unit, not just match the provider's amount. Sentence 7 suggests floor/truncate as a fix rather than stating it as fact, and the checkpoint reference in sentence 1 seems off.

What I want instead is a generic rule: any quoted string in a sentence must be a verbatim substring of the evidence (request, steps, diff, outlines, or message) — that gives a strong, checkable truth constraint without requiring semantic judgment.

I'm now thinking through thresholds: quotes need to be long enough (maybe 15-20 characters) to avoid false positives from short JSON tokens, and I should check them as normalized substrings across all evidence sources to handle formatting differences.

I'm deciding this quote-verification check belongs under item 3 — verbatim citation checking — since it surfaced directly from the rewriting I'm doing, and I'll fold it in as a small addition since it catches a real false claim rather than scope creep. I still need to handle truncated outline text with ellipses as a special case.

I'm refining the regex for detecting quoted text, specifically fixing a bug where apostrophes in possessive words like "customer's" and "agent's" could accidentally pair up and get misidentified as a long quoted span — adding boundary checks so the quote marks must be preceded/followed by whitespace or punctuation, not letters.

I need to worry about false positives from the regex matching unrelated in-between text that happens to be long and contain enough spaces—like filler text between two unrelated quoted JSON values getting mistaken for an actual prose quotation, which would trigger a false objection since that span wouldn't match anything in the evidence.

The fix is to use proper non-overlapping pairwise matching—just find all quoted substrings sequentially with findall, which naturally pairs quotes in order rather than mixing between-quote content, then filter those results by length and spacing thresholds. I'd apply the same guarded approach for single quotes and curly quotes.

I also need to handle unresolved quotes as an evidence-resolution objection, similar to how IDs are checked, folding it into check_citations' unresolved list and building the haystack from all the evidence fields—request, message, steps, diff, outlines, comparison, subject—while excluding the symptom since it's passed separately.

For symptom handling, I'll add an optional parameter so quotes drawn from it don't get wrongly flagged. Then normalization needs to lowercase, collapse whitespace, unify quote characters, strip punctuation, and handle ellipsis-split pieces, matching truncated outlines and multi-line requests consistently. I want to test this against the existing six briefs to see how well the matching holds up in practice.

cat >> hackathon.md <<'EOF'

### 2:35 PM, an id inside a sentence has to be real too

The review was right on both counts. The `cents-off` brief said "as shown in span ad7eeb7e" and cited `ad7edb7e`. The citation was real and the id in the sentence was one character off, and the check only looked at citations. The same brief said "Python's round() rounds 0.5 and above up", which is not how it treats a half.

What changed in the citation check:

- Any token in a sentence that looks like an id, eight or more hex characters with a digit in them, has to match something in the evidence. If it does not, the sentence is cut and the draft is sent back once, the same way as for the measured rate. Ids that do match are added to the sentence's citations.
- Words in quotation marks have to be in the evidence as quoted, once they are long enough to be a quotation. This was not on the review's list. It came from reading the rewrites: one said the request "did not ask for the recorded refund to differ", when the request's own words were "round the amount to the nearest whole unit before recording it". The model is now told to give the request in its own words, in quotes, and the quotes are checked.
- The model is told not to explain from memory how a language behaves, and that a commit may simply have done what was asked. The old instruction told it to say where the request and the commit part ways, which made it find a gap when there was none.
- When every run from the culprit on failed, the measurements now say that the estimate sits under 100% only because the replays are few. Before that, a rewrite spent a sentence on "the remaining 7% that may pass".

content.thinking:
Since traffic generation isn't tagged, the page can't detect from traces alone that eval/traffic.py sent the request, and I can't retroactively modify the agent code at historical commits to add a distinguishing tag—so I need another way to identify where tags actually originate.

I'm weighing whether to mark traffic runs via a flag, a tracked config file, or a note field in the Damages dataclass—leaning toward adding a simple `source` description to Damages since it's the most transparent and robust option without touching old commits.

Actually, I think adding a `traffic_sent_by` field to the Case model itself might work better: each case file could declare its traffic was generated by eval/traffic.py, and the fix() function could preserve this when rewriting case text. But I'm questioning whether provenance of traffic really belongs in a case file, since a case is meant to represent a symptom and failing inputs rather than metadata about simulated traffic.

With the case-file key settled, reruns via `whodunit casebook` need nothing extra since damages.source is just stored in the record. I'll settle on the `traffic_sent_by` field in the case object, documented as noting who sent the ordinary runs when they weren't real users — and the traffic line about prior ordinary runs should appear both in Suspects and Damages sections, pulling from that same stored value.

Now I'm drafting the Damages page text: noting how many ordinary runs failed this case's check and what refund amount resulted, clarifying these runs came from eval/traffic.py simulating customers in test currency with no real customer involved, then adding scale context on total ordinary runs recorded for the culprit and later commits, including how many errored for unrelated reasons. I'm deciding to keep that context line small since it just explains exclusions rather than counting additional damage.

I'm now thinking it's simpler to drop the "bad-for-any-reason" count from the page entirely and just state denominators plainly: total ordinary runs on record, and how many specifically asked what this case's check asks. In the underlying record, I'd keep the raw run counts but consider renaming or removing the "bad_runs" style fields since they conflate unrelated regressions with this case's actual damage.

I'm redesigning the Damages fields to separate general run/cost context from case-specific outcomes — tracking ordinary runs, tokens, and cost separately from case_runs, case_bad, wrongly_paid, withheld, and the cost specifically tied to runs that failed this case's check, plus replay runs and who sent them. I also need to make the render code tolerant of older evidence snapshots that use the old damages schema, since those are static and won't be migrated.

For the business-plan doc, I'm clarifying the wording so it's clear the "measured" numbers come from scripted traffic generated by eval/traffic.py rather than real customer traffic, and that unit costs are based on replay measurements of our own runs. I'm also confirming that "fail this case's own check" is specific to the refund-counting logic, which matches how the README describes this agent's checks.

I'm also being careful about editing whodunit files while a background simulation is running, since each case spawns a new process and AGENTS.md warns against modifying that code mid-run.

"""Damages: only runs that fail the case's own check are this case's damage."""

import json
import sqlite3

from whodunit import damages

CULPRIT, LATER, EARLIER = "c" * 40, "d" * 40, "a" * 40
ASKED = "Hi, I'm cust_6. Could I get a refund of 30 dollars for order 2002? Thanks."


class Traces:
    """Stands in for neatroots: answers query_sql from a small SQLite database with the same two tables."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
        self.db.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
        self.db.execute("create table runs (trace_id, workflow, doctor, status, error_count, finding_count, started_ms, input_preview)")
        self.db.execute("create table spans (trace_id, name, span_kind, attributes, output_preview, status_code, model, prompt_tokens, completion_tokens)")
        self.count = 0

    def run(self, commit, asked, refunds=(), case="", status="ok", findings=0, tokens=(1000, 100)):
        self.count += 1
        trace = f"t{self.count:031d}"
        tags = f"commit:{commit}" + (f" case:{case}" if case else "")
        self.db.execute("insert into runs values (?, 'refund-agent', 0, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", (trace, status, int(status == "error"), findings, self.count * 1000.0, asked))
        self.db.execute("insert into spans values (?, 'run_info', 'CHAIN', ?, '{}', 0, null, 0, 0)", (trace, tags))
        self.db.execute("insert into spans values (?, 'chat', 'LLM', '', '', 0, 'claude-haiku', ?, ?)", (trace, *tokens))
        for order, amount in refunds:
            self.db.execute("insert into spans values (?, 'issue_refund', 'TOOL', '', ?, 0, null, 0, 0)", (trace, json.dumps({"order_id": order, "refunded": amount})))
        return trace

    def call(self, tool, sql):
        assert tool == "query_sql"
        return {"rows": [dict(row) for row in self.db.execute(sql)]}


def test_only_runs_that_fail_this_cases_check_are_its_damage():
    traces = Traces()
    traces.run(CULPRIT, ASKED, refunds=[("2002", 30.0)])  # this case's bug: someone else's order refunded
    traces.run(LATER, ASKED)  # the same request, and the agent refused, as it should
    traces.run(LATER, "Please refund order 3003 in full for customer cust_7.", refunds=[("3003", 130.0)], status="error", findings=1)  # another regression
    traces.run(LATER, "Please refund order 1001 for customer cust_9.", findings=1)  # a finding that has nothing to do with this case
    traces.run(EARLIER, ASKED, refunds=[("2002", 30.0)])  # before the culprit, so not in the window
    traces.run(CULPRIT, ASKED, refunds=[("2002", 30.0)], case="strangers-paid/1")  # Whodunit's own replay
    since_culprit = [CULPRIT, LATER]
    counted = damages.count(traces, "refund-agent", commits=since_culprit, case_id="strangers-paid")
    counted = damages.count_case(traces, counted, "refund-agent", since_culprit, [(ASKED, [])])
    assert counted.runs == 4 and counted.replay_runs == 1
    assert (counted.case_runs, counted.case_bad) == (2, 1)  # the two runs that errored or were flagged for other reasons are not counted
    assert (counted.wrongly_paid, counted.withheld) == (30.0, 0.0)
    assert counted.case_bad_tokens == 1100 and counted.case_bad_usd == round((1000 * 1.0 + 100 * 5.0) / 1e6, 4)
    assert not hasattr(counted, "bad_runs")  # "N of M runs went bad" lumped every regression together, and is gone


def test_money_owed_and_not_refunded_is_counted_too():
    traces = Traces()
    owed = "Hi, I'm cust_4. Please refund order 2002, I ordered the wrong item by mistake."
    traces.run(CULPRIT, owed)
    traces.run(CULPRIT, owed, refunds=[("2002", 30.0)])
    counted = damages.count_case(traces, damages.count(traces, "refund-agent", commits=[CULPRIT]), "refund-agent", [CULPRIT], [(owed, [{"order_id": "2002", "refunded": 30.0}])])
    assert (counted.case_runs, counted.case_bad, counted.withheld, counted.wrongly_paid) == (2, 1, 30.0, 0.0)
EOF

The replay counts are higher now than earlier in the whole-history case — likely because replay_runs matches on a case-tag pattern, and more runs have accumulated since the original counts were recorded.

Cost attribution needs actual tokens per tag, and fix-verification replays don't even store their own tags, only failed-replay text. The real problem is that a fresh rerun at the end of stage 2 would inflate the count further since it'd capture all prior runs under the same case id too — so counting by case-id tag alone is fundamentally broken; I need to scope by time, using the first replay's start timestamp as a boundary for what counts as "this investigation's" replays.

Querying by exact tags could balloon into hundreds of SQL ORs, so chunking tags into batches of 50 seems more practical. The simplest robust approach is really just a time window plus case id: record the earliest replay start per record, and for the upper bound use the latest known replay end already stored, so reruns of damages count the same replays as before.

For attempts, I need their replay times stored too, but existing records don't have those replays saved — though I can sanity-check against the existing damages counts (65 = 21+30+8+6, which checks out) to confirm those historical numbers were correct before later experiments inflated things. So when re-running damages now, I should preserve those earlier replay_runs/replay_usd values rather than overwrite them with inflated new counts.

Looking at how damages.count works, replays get counted within a time window derived from the record — the "to" boundary uses closed_ms if present, otherwise now. For existing records I need to figure out the right "to" timestamp from the log history, since damages were computed right after the investigate run finished, and a later ablation run (without the entire-graph alibis) happened separately and shouldn't be folded into that window.

I'm trying to reconcile the counts: checks (regression replays) ran after the fix log, and 21+6+30=57 plus 8 check runs gets to 65 — suggesting damages were actually recounted after the checks ran, not immediately after the fix.

For the simplest fix going forward, I'll treat existing records as settled: restore the previously recorded replay_runs/replay_usd values as they stood before today's plain-bisect experiment and ablation, and use counted_until_ms as the upper bound wherever it already exists on a record. For records missing that field, I'll backfill it using the last known timestamp from the record file itself.

A more principled approach is to use the git commit time of each record's last change before today's session as the cutoff, then query the run counts bounded by that timestamp and check them against the earlier numbers I saw (50, 65, 74, 119, 240, 558). If they line up, that confirms the method works, so I'll pull the commit time at HEAD~4 and run that query via Python.

content.thinking:
I'm looking at the wrong-accusation rate as a share of accusations actually made, which turns out to be much higher than the overall error rate across all cases—especially at lower replay counts where it's running 15-46% before dropping to single digits by 240-320 replays.

The flaky-baseline cases with a 10% bug rate are especially bad: at 320 replays, 86% of its accusations are wrong, and it mostly just says "nobody" (94-100% of the time). The pooled error rate looks fine (2.5-4.4%, under the nominal 5%) but that's misleading since it's dominated by easy cells.

Comparing to the sealed cases with ~168 replays and clean baselines, the nearest simulator cell suggests about 15% of accusations would be wrong even there, despite having fewer suspects (11-15 vs 40) which should make it easier. That's a real caveat I need to flag for the "5 of 5 named, 0 wrong" result on the rare cases—the sim says that accuracy isn't guaranteed at that replay count and suspect pool size.

I'm planning a cheap extra sweep matching the sealed conditions more closely: 13 suspects, 12% bug rate, clean baseline, with budgets at 120/168/320, to get a more direct read on expected error rates. I'll run this after the main simulation to avoid resource contention.

Then I'm turning to why the 95% confidence bar doesn't actually deliver 95% reliability in harder cells — it comes down to prior mismatch. The uniform prior over culprit position is fine, but the prior on failure rates doesn't match the true underlying rates well, especially when the "bug" rate (10%) is close to the baseline flake rate (5%), causing the Beta(1,1) prior to miscalibrate the posterior.

This means the README needs updating — the current pitch claims an accusation only fires at 95% confidence, which is technically true of the posterior math but misleading since simulated precision is lower for rare, low-rate bugs. I'm drafting language for a "what it does not do yet" section: something like "for bugs that fail roughly 1 in 10 runs, accusations are less reliable than 95% implies — in simulation with 40 suspects, 15% of accusations were wrong at 160 replays even on a clean baseline, worsening further when good commits also flake 5% of the time." I'll finalize these numbers once the sim and charts finish, then run the sealed-like sweep and check status.

  """## Wrong accusations, out of accusations made

The first version of this page gave wrong accusations as a share of all cases, which ran from 0% to 7%. That flatters the method wherever it mostly names nobody. If it names a commit in 10 cases out of 500 and 5 of those are wrong, that is 1% of cases and half of its accusations. The second number is the one that says whether an accusation can be trusted, so `tables.md` now has it for every cell. Pooled over the ten budgets, for the statistical bisect:

| The bug fails | Good commits never fail | Good commits fail 5% of the time |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 100% | 0 of 4,515 wrong, 0% | 39 of 4,377, 0.9% |
| 80% | 43 of 4,130, 1.0% | 69 of 3,885, 1.8% |
| 60% | 67 of 3,652, 1.8% | 127 of 3,290, 3.9% |
| 40% | 99 of 3,010, 3.3% | 156 of 2,420, 6.4% |
| 30% | 105 of 2,516, 4.2% | 132 of 1,655, 8.0% |
| 20% | 112 of 1,824, 6.1% | 132 of 725, 18.2% |
| 10% | 74 of 685, 10.8% | 74 of 92, 80.4% |

So "named at 95%" means what it says for bugs that fail about a third of the time or more. Below that it does not. For a bug that fails one run in ten on a clean baseline, about one accusation in nine is wrong across the budgets, and the small budgets are the worst: 11 wrong of 40 at 120 replays, 13 of 85 at 160, 17 of 318 at 320. When good commits also fail 5% of the time, a 10% bug is out of reach. The statistical bisect names nobody in 94% of cases even with 320 replays, 25 of the 29 commits it does name are innocent, and its top suspect is right in 11% of cases.

For comparison, plain bisect always names someone, so its wrong accusations are simply its wrong answers: 19% of them on a clean baseline across the whole grid, and 80% when good commits fail 5% of the time.

The model's own probability is off here because its priors are. It takes the failure rate of good commits to be about 5% and anything from rare to always for bad ones, so a rate of 10% sits closer to its idea of a good commit than of a bad one, and a few stray failures in a row can look like a change point.

### The sealed eval's two rare cases

Two of the five sealed cases fail about 12% and 14% of the time. Both went unnamed at 120 replays and were named, correctly, at 168. `short-range.json` simulates cases shaped like them: 13 suspects, a clean baseline, a bug that fails 12% of the time, 2,000 cases per row.

| Replays allowed | Named and right | Named and wrong | Nobody named | Wrong, of accusations made |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 120 | 24% | 3.6% | 72% | 71 of 554, 13% |
| 168 | 46% | 3.4% | 51% | 68 of 978, 7% |
| 320 | 77% | 3.5% | 20% | 69 of 1,607, 4% |

Those cases were allowed up to 320 replays. With that much, an accusation in conditions like theirs is wrong about one time in 23, close to what the 95% bar promises. With only 120 it would have been wrong about one time in eight. The eval's result, five named and none wrongly, fits this and is far too small to confirm it.

The ablation results aren't saved anywhere permanent, so I need to pull the numbers from the build log: 30 replays across 8 commits hit 95.4%, versus 20 replays across 5 commits at 99.8%, each tested once. I'll add a record field capturing this comparison, storing replay counts, commits tested, and probability for the "without head start" case.

The harder question is how the pipeline generates and preserves this ablation data. Since the whole-history case gets rerun fresh at stage 2 and its record regenerated, the ablation note needs to live separately and survive that regeneration — maybe as its own record file under an `eval/ablation/` directory, linked back to the main case rather than dropped into the casebook's glob pattern where it'd be mistaken for another case.

Actually, running three separate ablation configurations (both effects, alibis only, traffic only, neither) at ~10 cents each would be noisy with single runs. A cleaner approach is to simulate the statistical bisection 2000 times with the real priors (57 suspects, 22 alibi weights, culprit at position 37) with and without priors, which gives a free and more reliable estimate of what alibis actually save than one noisy real run per condition.

For the actual page copy, I'll use the honest framing from the one real ablation run: 30 replays across 8 commits to 95.4% without the head start versus 20 across 5 with it, noting clearly that this run removed both alibis and traffic together, so the savings can't be cleanly attributed to either alone. I'll store this as a `"without_head_start"` key in the record.

Since the original record wasn't kept, the simplest path is a small hand-entered tracked JSON file at `eval/ablation/whole-history.json` capturing the case name, replay count, commits tested, probability, what was removed, run count, and the source citation back to the build log entry.

I'll implement `--ablation` as a flag writing a sibling `<case>.ablation.json` with the replay stats, culprit, and probability, keeping it separate from the main record — for now I'll hand-enter numbers from the build log with a documented source, then regenerate it properly later for ten to fifteen cents once stage 2 finishes.

I also want to update the pitch/demo-script and README to add the alibi sentence, noting that "Entire's code graph gives 22 of the 57 commits an alibi" and that without that head start the same case took 30 replays instead of 20 in the one run tried — placing this both in the demo script and in the eval/sealed README near the existing alibi mention.

Now I'm mapping the ablation flags to their effects: `--no-graph` removes "alibis from entire-graph," `not from_traffic` removes "ordinary runs as evidence," and `no_priors` removes "any prior at all" — and I'm checking whether with `--no-graph` the path-filter prior on touching the target still applies, since the "without entire-graph alibis and without traffic" case likely maps to `--no-graph` combined with no `--from-traffic`.

For rendering, I'm adding a small paragraph after the alibi details in the Suspects section showing what the head start was worth, and writing tests confirming the ablation record renders "30 replays across 8 commits" and that `lineup --ablation` writes the file without altering the main record.

I'm clarifying the scope: user-facing content like pages, records, README, pitch, and evidence files should avoid naming any assistant, model, or vendor, while code can retain such strings only where actually required for API calls or commands—like in llm.py or the PRICES dictionary where keys must match model names.

For eval/ask.sh, the `claude -p` invocation is a required command, so that stays. In victims/refund-agent, the vendor reference is part of the victim's own API, also staying. Test fixtures referencing 'claude-haiku' or 'openai' are cheap to swap for neutral placeholders—I'll change the PRICES test to use a fake model with custom pricing, and the dependency-diff fixture from openai to httpx.

For AGENTS.md, it mentions qwen/Ollama, Haiku, OpenAI-compatible, and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY — these are tool facts that commands actually need, so I'll mostly leave them, though I might soften phrasing like "the small Haiku model" to something more generic like "the gateway's small model."

The victim's refund-agent README also names specific model identifiers, but since it's part of the victim's own grown history rather than the clean root README, editing it would add a commit at HEAD outside the eval/ask.sh flow — not necessarily harmful, but worth being cautious about since the cases rely on fixed SHAs distinguishing good from bad states.

I'd rather leave the victim untouched since its history is itself the eval artifact; I'll note in the log that I left it alone and why. The build log (hackathon.md) isn't explicitly in my item list, but it likely names assistants/models too — I should grep it and decide whether to neutralize it under the "repo text" writing rule covering README, pitch, scripts, comments. Checking the motive fields, I see agent 'Claude Code' and model 'claude-sonnet-5' recorded, which I'll need to decide how to handle.

I think the cleanest fix is to drop `agent` and `model` from the Motive record entirely rather than just blanking them, so the dataclass no longer carries assistant identity, and change the CLI print to something generic like "Asked of the coding agent at {time}". For brief.model ('claude-sonnet-4.6'), I'll replace it with a `written_by` field describing it as "a model" or "a fixed template" with a reason, renaming the test-referenced key from "model" to "writer" with values like "a model" or "a fixed template" plus an explanatory note.

I also need to scan evidence text more broadly — run_info outputs can contain model ids and span names like "openai.chat.completions.create", comparison text may name models, and even commit messages could leak "Co-Authored-By: Claude" lines. I should build a scrub function that strips known model ids and vendor names from all evidence text before it's gathered or written.

I should also scrub replay error reasons since stderr might leak vendor names like provider error types. The cleanest approach is a single chokepoint at save_record() in cli.py, recursively applying the neutral() scrubber to every string value before writing, which guarantees nothing downstream ever sees names—though I need to be careful it only touches name-like patterns and doesn't corrupt ids or keys.

One concern: the motive's verbatim quote check compares request text against the transcript, so if a request legitimately quotes something like "claude" as part of the user's own words, scrubbing would break that comparison—I'll need the check to run before scrubbing. For this repo's actual cases there aren't any such quoted names, so it's fine for now. I'll also add a one-off migration script to reload and re-save existing records through the scrubbed save_record, dropping motive.agent/model fields and renaming brief.model to writer.

This migration also needs to touch the evidence record files and the sealed/plain eval files, plus I should check what the brief page actually prints ("Written by: {model}") and update that template. I should also check lineup/damages/replays/rulings/cases files for any leaked names, and confirm pitch/README mentions are just sponsor handles and not model names—but the screenshots are a problem since old ones may literally show "claude-sonnet-4.6" baked into the image, meaning those need to be retaken.

Checking remaining files: `.claude/settings.json` and `eval/ask.sh` are legitimate code/config that should stay, and I need to glance at hackathon.md too. For neutral terminology, I'm deciding to map model tiers rather than raw IDs — haiku becomes "small model," sonnet becomes "larger model," opus becomes "largest model," which keeps things simple and readable in config output.

I also need patterns to catch other branded terms: "OpenAI" to "the model API," "Anthropic" to "the model provider," "Claude Code" to "the coding agent," and leftover "Claude" references to "the coding agent" as well. For standalone "Sonnet"/"Haiku"/"Opus" I'm being careful since "opus" can be an ordinary word, so I want to restrict matching to capitalized forms with optional version numbers to avoid false positives.

- Never run `entire enable` with `--import-history`. It would pull older sessions from this folder into the public record.

## How one case runs

1. Read neatlogs and neatroots to get the failing runs and the time the failures began.
2. List the suspect commits between the last good ref and the first bad one.
3. Replay the failing inputs against suspect commits in git worktrees. Agent failures are random, so repeat until the result is statistically confident.
4. Name the culprit and pull the Entire checkpoint behind it, which holds the original request and the session.
5. Ask the owner one question (revert, or keep the intent and patch) and remember the ruling.
6. Fix, replay to prove the fix, add the case as a permanent regression test, and open a PR or an Entire Trail.
7. Write the damage (bad runs and dollars) to cfo.ai.

Any description of the project opens with "which commit, and why". The fix comes after that.

## Layout

Python 3.12 through uv, in one repo.

- `whodunit/case.py`: a case is a symptom, the failing inputs, a good ref, a bad ref and a check.
- `whodunit/suspects.py`: the commits in `good..bad` with their Entire checkpoint ids. Commits that cannot reach the agent's code get a lower prior (path filter first, then entire-graph impact).
- `whodunit/replay.py`: one git worktree per commit under test. It runs the target's replay command with the case input, tags the run with the commit SHA and case id, and reads the verdict from neatroots findings or a local check. A commit that will not build is skipped, like `git bisect skip`.
- `whodunit/lineup.py`: the statistical bisect, described below.
- `whodunit/motive.py`: `entire checkpoint explain` and `entire why` for the culprit, which give the original request and the session.
- `whodunit/brief.py`: the model writes the root-cause brief from the culprit diff, the relevant slice of the session transcript and a diff of a failing run against a passing one. Every sentence cites a span id, a commit or a checkpoint.
- `whodunit/ruling.py`: the ask-once memory (revert or patch, per kind of change), stored as files in the repo and mirrored to Entire Brain.
- `whodunit/fix.py`: applies the fix on a branch, replays the case until the posterior says it is fixed, adds the case to `cases/` as a regression test, and opens the PR or Trail.
- `whodunit/damages.py`: counts bad runs and cost from traces and writes them to cfo.ai.
- `whodunit/casefile/`: the static HTML case file, which is the main demo surface, and the CLI command `whodunit open-case`.
- `whodunit/onset.py`: reads the agent's ordinary runs from neatroots and brackets the failure between a good and a bad ref with the same change-point model. `--cloud` asks neatlogs when a detection began firing.
- `whodunit/neat.py`, `whodunit/llm.py`, `whodunit/env.py`: the MCP client for neatroots and neatlogs, the one place a model is asked for text, and the `.env` loader.
- `whodunit/simulate.py` and `whodunit/chart.py`: the simulator and its SVG charts. Results live in `eval/simulator/`.
- `whodunit/cli.py`: the commands. Each step reads and writes one case record, `<case>.record.json`, next to the case file.
- `eval/`: `score.py` scores cases against a sealed answer key, `traffic.py` sends everyday requests through a history, and `SECOND-SESSION.md` briefs the session that grows the victim.
- `tests/planted.py`: throwaway histories with a known culprit (an overpayment, a lookup that fails one run in three, a prompt change that needs a real model).
- `victims/refund-agent/`: the demo target. It starts from the refund agent in neatroots' `examples/` (Apache-2.0, and the README must say so) and grows to 40 or more commits through real coding-agent requests in a separate session, so the history and its checkpoints are genuine.

### The statistical bisect

Model a single change point c. The failure rate is p_good before c and p_bad from c onward. Estimate both rates by running the two endpoints several times and keeping Beta posteriors. Hold a posterior over c. Each round, replay the commit with the highest expected information gain and update with the Bernoulli outcome. The even split is kept as an option and does about as well. The prior on the good rate is about 5%, loosely held, which matters far more than the choice of picker. Stop at 95% on one commit or when the replay budget runs out, and in the second case report the remaining suspects with their probabilities.

Unit-test it against a simulator. Publish the curve of accuracy against replay budget, next to plain bisect, at failure rates from 100% down to 10%, with wrong accusations counted against accusations made.

## Tool facts checked on 10 October 2026

### neatroots

Version 0.2.6 is installed at `~/.local/bin/neatroots` and serves on port 4100. It is a local collector with checks and replay, and its MCP endpoint is `http://localhost:4100/mcp`.

- Whole-agent replay: `neatroots rerun add <project> "<command>" --cwd <dir>`, then `neatroots replay <trace-id> [--input ...]`. The agent receives `NEATROOTS_REPLAY_INPUT`, `NEATROOTS_REPLAY_ID` and `NEATLOGS_ENDPOINT`.
- Checks are YAML files in `.neatroots/checks/`. The `rule` kinds (repeat, errors, count, threshold, match, run_end) need no model. `yes_no` questions return a probability and need neatroots' local model. On the evening of 10 October that model was found switched on (`qwen2.5:3b-16k` through Ollama on port 11434), and the built-in `ignored-tool-error` check now runs it on incoming runs. A burst of replays therefore queues model work on this machine, so keep replays to two or three at a time while it is on.
- `neatroots mock-llm` is a key-free stand-in LLM on port 4110.
- `neatroots status` reports "cloud no key", so importing cloud traces needs the project key configured first.
- MCP tools used here: `search_runs`, `get_run_outline`, `list_findings`, `compare_runs`, `rerun`, `replay`, `query_sql`, `import_cloud_trace`.

### neatlogs cloud

The MCP endpoint is `https://ingest.neatlogs.com/mcp` with the project key as a Bearer token. `search_traces` does full-text search over names, errors and metadata, and no tag filter is documented, so check early that a commit SHA stored in metadata can be searched. `get_trace_context` returns the span tree with inputs and outputs. `get_detection_trend` returns hour or day buckets and dates the onset of failures. The Python SDK needs Python 3.10 to 3.13, takes the Project API key (the `nlw_` key returns 401), and needs `neatlogs.flush()` before exit. `python -m neatlogs doctor --probe` checks the setup.

- Whole-agent replay: `neatroots rerun add <project> "<command>" --cwd <dir>`, then `neatroots replay <trace-id> [--input ...]`. The agent receives `NEATROOTS_REPLAY_INPUT`, `NEATROOTS_REPLAY_ID` and `NEATLOGS_ENDPOINT`.
- Checks are YAML files in `.neatroots/checks/`. The `rule` kinds (repeat, errors, count, threshold, match, run_end) need no model. `yes_no` questions return a probability and need neatroots' local model. On the evening of 10 October that model was found switched on (`qwen2.5:3b-16k` through Ollama on port 11434), and the built-in `ignored-tool-error` check now runs it on incoming runs. A burst of replays therefore queues model work on this machine, so keep replays to two or three at a time while it is on.
- `neatroots mock-llm` is a key-free stand-in LLM on port 4110.
- `neatroots status` reports "cloud no key", so importing cloud traces needs the project key configured first.
- MCP tools used here: `search_runs`, `get_run_outline`, `list_findings`, `compare_runs`, `rerun`, `replay`, `query_sql`, `import_cloud_trace`.

### neatlogs cloud

The MCP endpoint is `https://ingest.neatlogs.com/mcp` with the project key as a Bearer token. `search_traces` does full-text search over names, errors and metadata, and no tag filter is documented, so check early that a commit SHA stored in metadata can be searched. `get_trace_context` returns the span tree with inputs and outputs. `get_detection_trend` returns hour or day buckets and dates the onset of failures. The Python SDK needs Python 3.10 to 3.13, takes the Project API key (the `nlw_` key returns 401), and needs `neatlogs.flush()` before exit. `python -m neatlogs doctor --probe` checks the setup.

content.content:
## Models and spend

- Replays of the refund agent use the small Haiku model on the hackathon gateway (OpenAI-compatible, `LITELLM_BASE_URL` and `LITELLM_API_KEY` in `.env`, $20 budget). Three parallel calls on 10 October each returned in about 1.4 seconds with no throttling. The owner's own API key is the fallback and should be a one-setting switch.
- Most development runs should use `neatroots mock-llm` or a scripted fake LLM and cost nothing.
- Never change model or provider inside one case. The bisect compares failure rates across commits, and a model change would look like a regression.
- Investigation and fix run through the coding agent in headless mode. The repo must also work with a plain API key so other people can run it. Keep `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` out of the shell that launches the coding agent, and load `.env` only inside the replay code.
- Grading starts with neatroots rule checks, which use no model. The bisect itself uses no model.
- Keep investigations to about 10 before Sunday 11 October, 4:30 PM IST, and run the full eval after that.

## AWS

There is one shared $25 allowance and nothing meters it, so stop resources when they are idle. Use us-east-1 only, the pre-provisioned `Hackathon_VPC`, instance types t2, t3 or t3a from nano to large, and volumes of 50 GB or less. Only one EC2 instance may exist at a time, so terminate before replacing. Bedrock is not included. The plan is a single t3.large from Sunday evening as the replay worker and the host for the public case file page. Launching anything is the owner's call each time.

2. Sunday 3 AM: replay runner over worktrees. Plain bisect finds an always-failing planted bug across 20 commits.
3. Sunday 10 AM: the statistical bisect finds a bug that fails about 30% of the time, and the simulator chart is done. This milestone matters most.
4. Sunday 6 PM: motive, brief, ruling memory, fix and verify, case file page v1.
5. Monday 2 AM: sealed-key eval on the grown victim, neatlogs cloud link (the detection trend dates the onset), cfo.ai model through MCP, parallel replays on the AWS allowance.
6. Monday noon: stretch target, README, evidence folder.
7. Monday 6 PM: demo video, which opens on "57 commits, which one did it?" and names the culprit inside 30 seconds. Submit at 7 PM.

If milestone 3 slips past Sunday 2 PM, drop the stretch target and the AWS runner and keep everything else.

## Where things stand, Sunday 11 October, midday

Read this before the milestones above, which were written before the build started.

Done and committed locally:

- Milestones 1 to 4, and the eval part of 5. `hackathon.md` has every step, including what went wrong.
- The victim has a real history: 55 commits made through `eval/ask.sh`, one fresh coding session per request. Five regressions were planted by a second session and sealed. `eval/sealed/README.md` has the result: 5 of 5 named, no wrong accusations, 4 of 5 fixed and proven.
- `whodunit investigate` runs a whole case. `cases/whole-history.toml` is the headline run and the one the video should show.
- `pitch/` has the video script, post drafts and the business plan numbers.

Still to do, in order of points:

1. cfo.ai. Required, and nothing is in it yet. `.mcp.json` names the server. A new session in this folder should offer it, and the owner signs in. Build the plan from `pitch/business-plan.md`: pricing, costs, revenue and runway, with the three scenarios. Each write needs the owner's yes.
2. Screenshots from neatlogs cloud. 232 traffic runs are there and the `Execution Failed` detection has fired 27 times. The owner is signed in to the dashboard and this session is not.
3. The push. The owner still has to read the list of personal items in the transcripts: home folder path, connector names, the titles of the private notes index, and `ownerAccountUuid` and `ownerOrganizationUuid` in `bridge-session` entries. After the push, turn on GitHub Pages for `cases/` so the casebook has a public address, and collect the Entire checkpoint link for commit `ced2ecd21c3e`, checkpoint `bfbe27725663`.
4. The video, from `pitch/demo-script.md`.
5. More #neatHack posts, from `pitch/posts.md`.

Rules that came out of the build:

- Two sessions in this folder at once end up in each other's checkpoints. Do unrelated work, such as research, from another folder.
- Do not edit `whodunit/` while a long `whodunit` run is in flight. Each case starts a new process that picks up the edit.
- neatroots returns at most 200 rows per query. Use `select_all` in `whodunit/neat.py`.
- A fix is proven only when its failure rate is back within 5 points of the rate before the culprit. Do not loosen that.
- Gateway spend was about $14 of $20 at midday on Sunday. A full investigation costs 20 cents to a dollar, and a rare bug can cost several dollars.
- Entire Brain is not installed. Its installer is a script piped from the network into a shell, which needs the owner's yes.

## Case file design

This direction is a proposal and the owner has not signed it off yet.

The metaphor is a detective's typed case file with a two-colour typewriter ribbon.

I need to watch out though, since git sometimes auto-guesses identity from the system user/hostname with just a warning, which could mask the bug I'm trying to catch.

To force determinism I'd set GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL to a temp file with `useConfigOnly = true`, which disables git's auto-guessing entirely, so the commit will fail unless my fallback identity flags are present — then the test can assert the revert commit succeeds with the "whodunit" author identity.

I also need a second test confirming that when a real identity already exists in config, it's respected rather than overridden. One subtlety: my identity detection relies on `git config --get user.name`, but if only environment variables are set (GIT_AUTHOR_NAME/COMMITTER_NAME) without any config, author and committer could end up mismatched — I should check both env vars together before deciding whether an identity already "exists."

Stage 1 wrapped up at 16:57 IST, and since nothing's being pushed yet, I can skip the checkpoint explain step the AGENTS guidance mentions. Moving into stage 2 for the Sunday evening/night work, I need to follow the specified order, writing a failing test before each change, and trimming from the bottom of the list if time gets tight — starting with marking the chapter, then the first stage 2 item.

Looking at item 2.1: currently in whodunit/replay.py, any timeout or non-zero exit gets treated as a FAIL verdict. I need to add a VOID verdict instead for provider and network errors, so those get retried. The tricky part is the requirement that the refund agent exit with a specific code (listed in the case file, like 75) on these errors — but replays run historical commits of the agent in worktrees, so changing the agent's exit-code handling at HEAD won't retroactively fix how old commits behave when they hit a provider error (they'd likely just throw an unhandled exception and exit 1). I'm trying to figure out how this exit-code requirement can actually work given that constraint.

The only way this works across history is a fallback: alongside the specific exit codes, the case file also needs to list stderr patterns (things like APIConnectionError, APITimeoutError, RateLimitError, 502/503/504, connection refused) so that historical commits lacking the dedicated exit code can still be detected as VOID by matching their stderr output.

Checking how the agent at older commits handles LLM call failures — the OpenAI client has a timeout and retry setup added later, but there's no broad exception handling around the API call itself, just a JSONDecodeError catch, so an unhandled connection error would just traceback and exit 1. That confirms detection has to rely on stderr pattern matching for historical commits rather than exit codes. One hacky idea is using a sitecustomize.py injected via PYTHONPATH to install an exception hook that maps provider errors to a specific exit code without touching the historical agent code at all — clever, since it would apply uniformly across every commit.

I could try flushing the exit handlers manually before the hard exit, but that feels hacky. Simpler approach: just document two mechanisms in the case file, starting with a `void_exit_codes = [75]` setting that gets honored whenever the agent exits with that code, applied from the commit that introduces it onward.

The other mechanism, `void_stderr`, is for older commits before this change exists, and matches strings like API/connection errors against the tail of stderr on non-zero exits. The instruction wants the refund agent to exit with its own designated code for those cases, so I need to modify it accordingly — bearing in mind the victim's history is built from real coding-agent requests via a headless session script that costs real money on the owner's plan, not the gateway.

I'm weighing whether to add this commit myself directly. AGENTS.md's eval design wanted the Whodunit session kept out of the victim's git history while a separate session grew the refund agent, but that was specifically for preserving the sealed eval's integrity, which is already done — so editing the agent at HEAD now shouldn't compromise anything, since cases reference fixed SHAs rather than HEAD. Still, I need to check whether a change at HEAD would even matter for replays, since those run at old suspect/fix commits branching from an older bad ref, meaning a new exit code at HEAD likely wouldn't be exercised by any existing case.

So any new exit code is really aimed at future cases, not existing tests, which rely on stderr patterns instead. I consider whether injecting behavior at replay time via some environment mechanism could make it apply retroactively, but that would really be the harness forcing behavior rather than the agent itself exiting with its own code, which feels like the wrong approach. I think the more sensible path is to modify agent.py at HEAD to add a void verdict for provider and network errors, giving the agent its own distinct exit code for those cases as listed in the case file.

That means catching provider errors around the LLM call, printing a message to stderr, and exiting with a specific failure code like 75, with the case file listing void_exit_codes accordingly; older commits without this logic would still need to fall back on stderr pattern matching, and I'd document both approaches together. For actually committing this victim change, I need to go through the ask.sh workflow, which runs a headless coding-agent session and could incur costs against the owner's subscription or API — so I should check what account or key ask.sh actually uses before proceeding, since spending through the owner's personal login rather than the gateway budget would be a meaningful distinction worth flagging first.

Given that even a $0.30 request sits under the $1 threshold for needing explicit cost disclosure, but switching to the owner's key is a separate tripwire I should respect, I think it's safer to just make the victim edit directly in this session as a normal, free commit rather than routing through ask.sh — noting explicitly in the commit log that this change was made directly by this session rather than via the agent-request pipeline, and that it comes after each case's known-bad reference point. I'm also checking whether AGENTS.md actually forbids this kind of direct edit, and it seems not: a direct edit from me still produces a genuine coding-agent commit with its own checkpoint, consistent with how the victim repo's history is supposed to grow.

I also realize running ask.sh would start a second session in the same folder, which risks tangling checkpoints with my own session — another reason to just edit directly instead. Separately, I'm thinking through how a VOID verdict should be handled in the bisection logic: it needs to be distinct from a SKIP (which marks a commit unbuildable), treated more like "no observation" that gets retried with backoff, while making sure void results don't stealthily bypass the budget accounting and cause an infinite loop if the provider is down — so I want a cap on consecutive void rounds with a clear failure note, and I need to check how the plain bisect path propagates a persistent void result.

For plain_bisect, I'm deciding that a persistent VOID should fall into the same "cannot be judged" bucket as SKIP, since the existing logic already treats anything that isn't PASS/FAIL as skipped, which conveniently covers this case. Now I'm working through how void results should surface downstream: fix.verify should ignore voids in its pass/fail counts but report a clear note if too many consecutive voids occur, cli.check should report voided counts separately from failures, the statistical CLI's round display needs a "v" marker for void, and the resume logic needs to correctly build its evidence list while skipping over these void entries.

On the retry-timeout requirement, I'm planning to have the replay runner catch a timeout, retry once at double the limit, and only mark it a true failure if it times out again -- otherwise the original timeout gets dropped as a voided attempt and the retry's result stands, with a new `voided` field tracking how many attempts were discarded before the final verdict.

For void errors like provider/network failures, I'm adding a backoff retry policy (2s then 8s) up to two more attempts, and if every attempt voids, the final verdict becomes VOID with the provider error recorded as the reason. I also need to surface the voided count in the report and on the page, noting explicitly that a voided replay is never evidence, and I'm defining a helper to detect whether a given return code/stderr pattern qualifies as a void condition.

I should actually test this rather than guess—I'll check the agent code at HEAD and base, then run the agent with a fake LLM pointed at a closed port to see what stderr and exit code it actually produces. That's a cheap experiment to confirm real behavior.

def llm_settings() -> tuple[str, str, str]:
    """Return (base_url, api_key, model) for the chosen REFUND_LLM."""
    choice = os.environ.get("REFUND_LLM", "mock")
    if choice == "mock":  # neatroots mock-llm
        return os.environ.get("MOCK_LLM_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:4110/v1"), "mock", "mock"
    if choice == "fake":  # python fake_llm.py
        return os.environ.get("FAKE_LLM_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:4199/v1"), "fake", "fake"
    load_env_file()
    if choice == "gateway":
        return need("LITELLM_BASE_URL"), need("LITELLM_API_KEY"), "claude-haiku"
    if choice == "own":
        return "https://api.anthropic.com/v1/", need("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"), "claude-haiku-5-5"
    sys.exit(f"REFUND_LLM={choice} is not one of mock, fake, gateway, own.")


def trace_settings() -> tuple[str, str]:
    """Return (endpoint, api_key) for the chosen TRACE_TO."""
    choice = os.environ.get("TRACE_TO", "neatroots")
    if choice == "neatroots":
        # neatroots sets NEATLOGS_ENDPOINT itself when it replays the agent.
        return os.environ.get("NEATLOGS_ENDPOINT", "http://localhost:4100"), "neatroots-local"
    if choice == "neatlogs":
        load_env_file()
        return "https://ingest.neatlogs.com", need("NEATLOGS_API_KEY")
    sys.exit(f"TRACE_TO={choice} is not one of neatroots, neatlogs.")


@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=1)
def agent_version() -> str:
    import tomllib

    with open(HERE / "pyproject.toml", "rb") as f:
        return tomllib.load(f)["project"]["version"]


def current_commit() -> str:
    given = os.environ.get("WHODUNIT_COMMIT")
    if given:
        return given
    try:
        out = subprocess.run(["git", "rev-parse", "HEAD"], cwd=HERE, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=5)
        return out.stdout.strip() or "unknown"
    except (OSError, subprocess.SubprocessError):
        return "unknown"


def run_tags() -> list[str]:
    tags = [f"commit:{current_commit()}", f"llm:{os.environ.get('REFUND_LLM', 'mock')}"]
    for name, label in (("WHODUNIT_CASE", "case"), ("NEATROOTS_REPLAY_ID", "replay")):
        if os.environ.get(name):
            tags.append(f"{label}:{os.environ[name]}")
    return tags


LLM_BASE_URL, LLM_API_KEY, DEFAULT_MODEL = llm_settings()
MODEL = os.environ.get("REFUND_MODEL", DEFAULT_MODEL)
TRACE_ENDPOINT, TRACE_API_KEY = trace_settings()

import neatlogs  # noqa: E402
from neatlogs import span  # noqa: E402

TAGS = run_tags()

neatlogs.init(
    api_key=TRACE_API_KEY,
    endpoint=TRACE_ENDPOINT,
    workflow_name=os.environ.get("WORKFLOW", "refund-agent"),
    tags=TAGS,
    instrumentations=["openai"],
    flush_interval=0.2,
)

from openai import OpenAI  # noqa: E402  (import after neatlogs.init)

client = OpenAI(base_url=LLM_BASE_URL, api_key=LLM_API_KEY, timeout=30.0, max_retries=2)

SYSTEM_RULES = [
        "commit_short": current_commit()[:12],
        "model": MODEL,
        "version": agent_version(),
        "max_steps": max_steps,
    }


MODEL_CALLS = 0


@span(kind="WORKFLOW", name="refund")
def run(request: str, max_steps: int = 3):
    global MODEL_CALLS
    run_info(max_steps)
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": request}]
    for _ in range(max_steps):
        r = client.chat.completions.create(model=MODEL, messages=messages, tools=TOOLS, max_tokens=150)
        MODEL_CALLS += 1
        m = r.choices[0].message
        if not m.tool_calls:
            return m.content
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": m.content, "tool_calls": [tc.model_dump() for tc in m.tool_calls]})
        for tc in m.tool_calls:
            try:
                args = json.loads(tc.function.arguments or "{}")
            except json.JSONDecodeError as exc:
                timestamp = datetime.now().strftime("%H:%M:%S")
                print(f"[{timestamp}] tool {tc.function.name} got bad arguments: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
                content = json.dumps({"error": f"invalid arguments JSON: {exc}"})
            else:
                content = call_tool(tc.function.name, args)
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": tc.id, "content": content})
    return "I couldn't finish this one. A person will follow up with you shortly."


if __name__ == "__main__":
    args = [a for a in sys.argv[1:] if a not in ("--json", "--quiet")]
    request = os.environ.get("NEATROOTS_REPLAY_INPUT") or " ".join(args) or DEFAULT_REQUEST
    try:
        reply = run(request)
        if "--json" in sys.argv:
            print(json.dumps({"request": request, "reply": reply, "refunds": REFUNDS, "model": MODEL,
                              "model_calls": MODEL_CALLS}))
        elif "--quiet" not in sys.argv:
            print(reply)
    finally:
        neatlogs.flush()
        neatlogs.shutdown()
#!/bin/sh
# Send one request to a fresh headless coding session and report the commit it made.
#
#   eval/ask.sh "Add a status field to each order and commit."
#
# Each call is its own session, so Entire records the request as the motive for the commit.
# WORKER_MODEL picks the model (default sonnet). The request should end by asking for a commit.
set -u
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." || exit 2
if [ -n "$(git status --porcelain -- victims/refund-agent)" ]; then
  echo "victims/refund-agent has uncommitted changes. Commit or discard them first."
  exit 2
fi
before=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
out=$(claude -p "$1" \
  --model "${WORKER_MODEL:-sonnet}" \
  --permission-mode acceptEdits \
  --settings '{"includeCoAuthoredBy": false, "attribution": {"commit": "", "pr": ""}}' \
  --append-system-prompt "Work only inside victims/refund-agent. Commit messages carry no co-author trailer and no generated-with line. Make exactly one commit for this request." \
  --allowedTools "Read" "Edit" "Write" "Glob" "Grep" "Bash(git add:*)" "Bash(git commit:*)" "Bash(git status:*)" "Bash(git diff:*)" "Bash(git log:*)" "Bash(uv run:*)" "Bash(uv add:*)" "Bash(uv lock:*)" "Bash(python3 -m py_compile:*)" \
  --max-budget-usd "${WORKER_BUDGET:-1.5}" --output-format json 2>/dev/null | tail -1)
after=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
cost=$(printf '%s' "$out" | python3 -c "import json,sys
try: print(round(json.load(sys.stdin).get('total_cost_usd', 0), 2))
except Exception: print('unknown')")
if [ "$before" = "$after" ]; then
  # Nothing was committed. Put the agent's folder back so the next request starts clean.
  git checkout -q -- victims/refund-agent 2>/dev/null
  git clean -fdq -- victims/refund-agent 2>/dev/null
  echo "no commit was made (cost $cost). The folder was put back as it was."
  exit 1
fi
if git log -1 --format=%B | grep -qi "^co-authored-by"; then
  git log -1 --format=%B | grep -vi "^co-authored-by" > .git/whodunit-msg && git commit -q --amend -F .git/whodunit-msg
fi
echo "$(git rev-list --count "$before"..HEAD) commit(s), cost $cost:"
git log --format='%H %s' "$before"..HEAD
git show --stat --format= HEAD | tail -1
